ca_jaws_vicinity.blurb: A small cluster of granite boulders on Mount Woodson in north San Diego County, sitting a bit above 2,300 feet along the road that climbs the hill. Most of the twenty problems are bouldering, with a few top-rope laps and a single trad line mixed in. The grades split into two camps: a good handful of easy problems from V0 to V2, then a short run of serious V7 and harder testpieces, so it suits strong boulderers more than a casual crowd. The stone is the compact, short-climb granite the mountain is known for. Expect to wander a little to find the blocks, as the hillside holds hundreds of boulders.

ca_cyanide_gully.blurb: A sun-soaked set of granodiorite cliffs high in Pine Creek Canyon above Bishop, at roughly 7,500 feet. Trad and sport lines share the walls, with a fair number of routes that can go either way, and the quality of the rock is good throughout. Grades start around 5.8 and are centred on 5.10 and 5.11, with a few hard 5.12 and 5.13 lines at the top end, so it rewards intermediate to strong climbers. Because the faces catch the sun most of the day, it is at its best when the weather is cool and gets hot fast in summer. It tends to be quieter than the canyon's busier walls. Many routes finish with a rappel or a loose walk-off, and a helmet is wise.
ca_cyanide_gully.approach: Follow the canyon approach to a point about 1.1 miles beyond the turnoff for the next gully down, cross the creek on a narrow beam, go up a short road or ramp, then head straight up the talus to the cliffs.

ca_cougar_crag_west.blurb: The western half of a twin pair of small crags in north San Diego County, low down at about 500 feet near the Temecula end of the county. It holds twenty routes, mostly traditionally protected single pitches with a couple of top-rope lines and one bolted route. The grades are friendly: most climbs sit between 5.7 and 5.10, with a few easier ones, which makes it a good place for newer trad leaders to build mileage. The walls are short and the anchors can generally be reached by scrambling. The footpath up to the base is steep and very loose, so sturdy boots help.

ca_fun_house_the_2.blurb: A friendly slab wall in the Bowman Valley, a quiet group of granite crags below a dam in the Sierra foothills northeast of Nevada City, at about 5,400 feet. Twenty climbs here, mostly bolted sport routes along with a few top-ropes, a handful of short boulder problems and one trad line. Grades run from 5.6 to 5.10, with the bulk in the 5.7 to 5.9 range, and the slabs are textured but can turn thin on the harder lines. It is a popular warm-up spot before heading to the steeper walls nearby, and a sound choice for beginners. The walk in from the road takes about a minute.
ca_fun_house_the_2.parking_note: Drive Bowman Lake Road off Highway 20 to the bridge below the dam and leave the car in the wide spot just before it, beside the chained-off road that heads toward the dam. The last stretch of the road is gravel and rough in places.

ca_echo_rock_south_face.blurb: A compact sun-facing wall at the south end of Echo Rock in the middle of Joshua Tree National Park, at about 4,250 feet. Twenty climbs are packed into a small space, mostly trad crack and face lines, with four bolted routes. The grades climb steadily from 5.8 through a big cluster of 5.10 and 5.11, and reach up to low 5.13, so it works for solid intermediates and strong specialists alike. The granite is coarse and sometimes fractured near the base. Being sheltered and warm, it is a good option on a cold or blustery day, while in hot weather you want to climb in the morning.

ca_old_woman_west_face_the.blurb: The west side of the Old Woman formation, in the Hidden Valley area of Joshua Tree National Park at about 4,200 feet. It is among the easiest crags in the park to reach, on a short trail from the Hidden Valley day-use lot or from inside the campground. About twenty routes, nearly all single-pitch trad, with a couple of top-ropes and one bolted line. The grades are weighted toward 5.10, with some 5.7 to 5.9 routes for warm-ups and a few harder 5.11 and 5.12 lines. Climbs mix cracks and face moves on granite and sometimes finish with smears. Traffic on lesser-known lines is light, and an early start avoids the desert heat.

ca_bubble_the.blurb: A popular sport crag high on Mount St. Helena above Calistoga, in California's wine country, at about 2,950 feet. The stone is a rough, pocketed volcanic rock with hueco-like holes, some of it vertical, some overhanging, and an easier slab section on the left. Seventeen of the twenty routes are bolted sport lines, with a few trad options. Grades run from 5.5 up to 5.11, and the largest group sits at 5.11, with several 5.10s, so it is better for climbers who already lead moderately hard. The left side holds shade until late morning, while the middle of the day brings heat, so early starts and spring or fall visits work well. It is the easiest of the mountain's crags to reach and gets steady traffic.
